question: What is the meaning of model number in relation to product identification?
description: The model number is a unique identifier assigned to a product to distinguish it from other products of the same type. It is often used in product identification and tracking throughout the product lifecycle, from manufacturing to end-of-life management. The model number can change over time, reflecting updates or modifications to the product design or specifications. This dynamic nature is captured by the AgentRole pattern, which allows us to separate the agent (manufacturer) from the role (model number) they are playing regarding the product. The model number is an essential attribute in the ProductSpecification class, enabling traceability and accountability for products.

A product is usually manufactured by a ‘manufacturer’, sold by 
‘vendors’, certified by ‘certification bodies’, and bought by ‘customers’. 
These roles around the product can change over time and are context- 
specific. The AgentRole pattern is suitable for capturing these dy­
namics, which allows us to separate the ‘Agent’ from the ‘Role’ they are 
playing regarding the product. For example, the manufacturer of a 
product is an agent who plays the role of a producer. This role has a 
temporal extent, which starts at the manufacturing date and continues 
until the discontinuation date of the product model. The ‘certification 
body’ is an agent that performs the role of a certifier for a limited 
‘temporal extent’, which is generally defined by the validity of the cer­
tificate (see Fig. 4). 
The product module also aims to model various aspects of products, 
including their specifications, manufacturing details, and supply chain 
information in order to enable traceability. Products often require 
traceability for supply chain and end of life management, quality 
assurance, and compliance. The ‘Provenance’ pattern is chosen to model 
the history, origin, or source of products, including how they are 
created, modified, and transferred. For example, to trace the product's 
manufacturing process, a ‘ProvenanceActivity’ instance can be created. 
Our ‘Product’ module can be linked to the ‘ProvenanceActivity’ using 
‘generatedBy’. This is addressed by making the Product class a subclass of 
the ‘EntityWithProvenance’. To trace the supply chain, we created a class 
of ‘SupplyChainActivity’ as a subclass of ‘ProvenanceActivity’. A product 
goes through multiple stages: raw material extraction, manufacturing, 
assembly, packaging, shipping etc. Each stage can be modeled as an 
instance of ‘SupplyChainActivity’. Using ‘generatedBy’, the product can be 
linked to these stages, thereby tracking its journey from raw materials to 
consumer. By using the ‘Provenance’ pattern in this manner, it is possible 
to provide a rich historical context to the entities in our DPP ontology, 
which is invaluable for providing information related to traceability, 
accountability, or detailed historical records of products. Fig. 4 shows 
both the product agent and provenance notion. 
Products involve various types of quantities like dimension, weight, 
density, and other similar technical specifications, for which the 
‘Quantity’ pattern is selected. To capture these key attributes, we 
specialized the class of ‘Product’ with the class of ‘ProductSpecification’. 
We introduced a property ‘hasQuantity’ to connect ‘ProductSpecification’ 
with ‘Quantity’. The ‘Quantity’ pattern makes it possible to specify the 
kind or type of the quantity. For example, ‘Length’, ‘Density’ or ‘Weight’ 
would be different kinds of quantities. The numerical value associated 
with a quantity typically consists of a unit and a number. The ‘Quantity’ 
pattern is well suited to capture these attributes in interoperable and 
scalable manner (see Fig. 5). 
A product may have different types or modification of existing types. 
The ‘Explicit Typing’ pattern is selected to explicitly define types for 
each product (see Fig. 5). 
Products often involve instructions such as assembly, disassembly 
and installation. Instructions might not always be simple strings. 
Directly linking a product to its assembly, disassembly, and installation 
instructions using datatype properties cannot capture additional 
contextual information, complexities, or relationships that could be

associated with each type of instruction. It might be necessary to capture 
more information about an instruction such as the tools required, the 
time it takes, the person or role responsible for the instruction. For 
example, the assembly instruction for a product might differ based on 
model or version of the product, or depending on the region or climate it 
is being assembled in. Using the ‘Property Reification’ pattern makes it 
possible to link an instruction to its specific context. Some instructions 
may involve a step-by-step guide. The ‘Sequence’ pattern is selected to 
model the involved steps (see Fig. 5). 
With the Product module from Blomqvist et al. (2023), we are also 
able to create a detailed representation related to products, their com­
ponents, and compositions. It enables to model products manufactured 
in batches and specifying the amount of each component or material 
within a product. Our Product module has similar attributes and re­
lationships and we modeled it as a specialization of the Product module 
from Blomqvist et al. (2023) (see Fig. 6). 
All the above patterns selected for the Product module are combined 
and shown in supplementary information S4. The Schema diagram also 
shows some of the identified key notions that are directly linked to the 
Product module. 
4.3.3.1.2. Material. The term ‘resource’, as it is defined in ISO/DIS 
59004, is synonymous with “raw material”, “feedstock”, “material” or 
“component. In this context, the definition of resource is adopted for our 
‘Material’ key notion, which is an “asset from which a solution is created or 
implemented”. This standard defines solution as “product, service or a 
combination thereof, that fulfills a need”. We aligned our ‘Material’ key 
notion with the MAT's Material defined as “a homogeneous or inhomo­
geneous substance that can be used to form elements (physical products or 
their components.” Given the broad scope of the material definition we 
adopted from the ISO/DIS 59904, we introduced the mat:Material from 
MAT as a specialization of our ‘Material’ key notion. Table 7 provides the 
summary of how our ‘Material’ key notion aligns with Material from 
MAT. 
Following the IRs identified from literature and interviews, and the 
EC proposals for DPPs, the material module we introduced incorporates 
properties, relationships, and attributes associated with different types 
of materials. We started by first employing the ‘Name Stub’ and ‘Identi­
fier’ modules to identify materials by their names and unique identifiers 
(see Fig. 8). 
‘Explicit Typing’ pattern is selected to capture information related to 
the types or categories of materials such as metal, plastic or composite. 
This pattern allows for more straightforward classification and querying. 
It can also be used to categorize various types of material properties such 
as mechanical, chemical, etc., without the need to create a large number 
of subclasses (see Fig. 7). 
Tracking the lifecycle of materials is crucial for a circular economy. 
The ‘Provenance’ pattern enables to track materials by keeping record of 
their origin, how they have been treated and used, and where they end 
up. This is critical information for recycling or repurposing of materials. 
To capture the provenance information, we introduced the Material 
class as a specialized version of “EntityWithProvenance”. With this 
pattern, we can capture information about how the material is made 
using the ‘generatedBy’ property and who is responsible for the creating 
or manufacturing the material using the ‘attributedTo’ property. Using 
the ‘used’ property, we can indicate that something was utilized in the 
process of creating something else, in our case, what materials or com­
ponents were involved in making a final product. Additionally, the 
‘wasDerivedFrom’ makes it possible to model the historical context of 
materials by capturing information about from where or what the ma­
terial is originated from. The ‘AgentRole’ pattern also provides more 
context to model information related to agents and the roles they play to 
create and use materials along with the temporal information. Infor­
mation related to provenance activities undertaken in the making of
